# A valid geometric chord certificate for sampled joint log-concavity

This is an auxiliary theorem, not a proof of the proposed mixed-integer
bound for the whole sampled log-concave class. It identifies an exact
transport-free consequence of joint log-concavity that controls oblique
cuts. The last section records the limitation of the certificate.

Let `f:R^n x R^d->[0,infinity)` be jointly log-concave, with `d>=1`.
Assume each sampled positive-mass fiber density is integrable and has
full-dimensional support, and the finite or countable sampled total
`M=sum_{z in Z^n} int f(z,x) dx` is finite and positive. Write `m_z` for
the individual fiber mass. The sampled probability measure is

    mu(A)=M^{-1} sum_z int 1_A(z,x) f(z,x) dx.

Use all closed ambient halfspaces in the definition of depth. The
continuous optimal-depth theorem in `candidate 0f025bdf9a51573b` gives,
for each positive fiber, a deterministic point `c_z` in the interior of
its convex support such that every containing continuous halfspace has
fiber mass at least `gamma_d m_z`.

## Midpoint lemma

Let `u,v` be distinct indices of the same parity and positive masses
`a=m_u,b=m_v`; put `m=(u+v)/2` and `c=(c_u+c_v)/2`. Then `(m,c)` is in
the positive support of `f`, and its sampled depth is at least

    gamma_d/M [sqrt(ab)+min(a,b)].                  (1)

For a through-point halfspace write

    H={ (z,x):alpha dot(z-m)+beta dot(x-c)>=0 }.

If `beta!=0`, set

    g_u(x)=f(u,x) 1_{beta dot(x-c_u)>=0},
    g_v(x)=f(v,x) 1_{beta dot(x-c_v)>=0},
    h(x)=f(m,x) 1_{beta dot(x-c)>=0}.

Joint log-concavity gives, for every `x,y`,

    h((x+y)/2)>=sqrt(g_u(x)g_v(y)).

Indeed the inequality is trivial if the right side is zero. Otherwise
both centered scalar products are nonnegative, their average is
nonnegative, and joint log-concavity applies at the midpoint in all
coordinates. By the standard Prekopa-Leindler inequality,

    int h >= sqrt(int g_u int g_v)>=gamma_d sqrt(ab).

The signed halfspace values at `(u,c_u)` and `(v,c_v)` sum to zero, so
at least one of these endpoint points belongs to `H`. The corresponding
endpoint contribution is at least `gamma_d min(a,b)`. It lies in a fiber
different from the midpoint, so the two contributions add. If `beta=0`,
use whole fiber densities and apply Prekopa-Leindler to them; the same
weaker lower bound remains valid. Through-point caps suffice by inward
translation. This proves (1), with closed boundaries included.

The center belongs to the positive support because the endpoint centers
have strictly positive density in the interiors of their supports, and
joint log-concavity gives a strictly positive value at their midpoint.
There is no rounding and no replacement of fiber sums by an integral.

## Integer-chord lemma

More generally suppose

    z_j=u+(j/L)(v-u) in Z^n, j=0,...,L,
    t_j=j/L, c_j=(1-t_j)c_u+t_j c_v,
    w_j=a^{1-t_j}b^{t_j}.

For every `i` the point `(z_i,c_i)` has depth at least

    gamma_d/M min(sum_{j=0}^i w_j,sum_{j=i}^L w_j). (2)

The signed halfspace values on the affine chain `(z_j,c_j)` form an
affine sequence. Hence indices where they are nonnegative form a prefix,
a suffix, or the entire chain; if the halfspace contains the selected
point, the corresponding sum of `w_j` is at least the displayed minimum.
At each captured index, the same positive-half endpoint truncations and
the `t_j` version of Prekopa-Leindler give cap mass at least

    (gamma_d a)^{1-t_j}(gamma_d b)^{t_j}
      =gamma_d w_j.

These are distinct integer fibers and their masses add. The endpoint
indices themselves use their continuous depth guarantees directly.
This proves (2), including every oblique normal.

## Equal endpoint mass consequence

For exactly three consecutive positive-mass fibers in `n=1`, if the two
endpoint masses both equal `a`, the sampled jointly log-concave class
does satisfy the target `gamma_d/2`. If the middle mass is `c>=2a`,
its continuous optimal point alone gives `gamma_d c/M>=gamma_d/2`.
If `c<=2a`, (1) gives `2 gamma_d a/M>=gamma_d/2`. No equality of the
fiber shapes, no affine map of their centers, and no uniformity of their
conditional densities is assumed.

The same certificate permits different endpoint shapes and different
pointwise density heights, as long as the integrated masses are equal.
In particular it applies to exponential tilts of uniform convex bodies
when the tilt balances the two endpoint fiber masses.

## Why this is not the general induction invariant

The marginal masses of a jointly log-concave density are log-concave by
Prekopa. Even for the strictly positive log-concave four-term sequence

    (m_0,m_1,m_2,m_3)=(1,100,100,1), M=202,

the largest single-fiber mass is only `100<M/2`. For every two-endpoint
chord in this sequence, the best lower bound supplied by the minimum
geometric-tail sum in (2) is at most `100`, also below `M/2=101`:
the adjacent high pair gives exactly 100; each high-low length-two chord
has weights `(1,10,100)` or its reverse and maximum minimum-tail sum
100; the outer length-three chord has four unit weights and maximum
minimum-tail sum two; the remaining adjacent high-low pairs give 100.

Such a marginal sequence is realizable by a jointly log-concave density:
take a piecewise affine concave function `ell(z)` on `[0,3]` with values
`0,log100,log100,0` at its integer points and put
`f(z,x)=exp(ell(z)) g(x) 1_{[0,3]}(z)` for any log-concave probability
density `g`. Thus the numerical limitation is not a marginal sequence
outside the sampled class. The actual product example has adequate
depth; it only demonstrates that no selection among these isolated
single-fiber and endpoint-chord certificates proves the general bound.

Finally, fiberwise Ball radialization does not automatically yield a
jointly convex body. Already for `n=d=1`, the jointly log-concave density
`f(z,x)=exp(z) 1_{[0,2]x[-1,1]}(z,x)` has radial integral fiber
`[-exp(z),exp(z)]` about zero. The midpoint of `(0,1)` and `(2,exp(2))`
has continuous coordinate `(1+exp(2))/2>exp(1)`, outside its middle
fiber. This explicitly invalidates joint convexity of that natural
mass-preserving fiberwise radialization.
